prompt: Use the provided painting as the reference for the brush hand: the same painter, the same sumi ink, the same warm rice paper. Paint the same red-crowned crane again, now standing at rest, as a bold freehand sumi-e painting made with a large soft brush in very few strokes. One crane stands still on two thin legs in shallow water, seen from the side, facing left, its beak pointing left, its long neck in a gentle S curve, its wings folded against the body. Anatomically correct: one head, one long beak, exactly two thin legs. The neck is one loaded, wet, jet-black calligraphic stroke that runs from the throat down to the breast. The tail plumes, the folded black flight feathers that hang over the tail on the right side of the bird, are five or six broad, heavy, jet-black strokes that end in split dry-brush tips. The white body is bare unpainted paper, held by one confident contour line that swells and thins and breaks like a line of calligraphy, with only two or three broad pale grey wet wash strokes under the wing and along the belly. Each leg is one quick thin dark stroke with a small knot at the joint. The small crown on top of the head is a tiny touch of gold leaf, never red. At the feet there are three thin reed stems, each drawn in a single quick stroke, and the faintest pale horizontal wash where the legs meet the water, and nothing else. The silhouette must read clearly from far away: a bold black neck, a white body, a bold black tail. No fine feather detail, no stippling, no hatching, no pencil line, no thin even outline, not a soft watercolour illustration. The whole bird is inside the frame, centred, filling about three quarters of the frame's height, with clear empty paper margins on every side and nothing cut off. Plain empty warm rice paper ground, evenly lit. No mountains, no mist, no sun, no text, no seal, no signature, no border. Nothing red anywhere.
